newsitem.title: USA: KAL flight recorders in "excellent condition".
newsitem.headline: KAL flight recorders in "excellent condition".

text.p: The flight recorders recovered from the wreckage of Korean Air Lines Flight 801 in Guam were virtually undamaged and could hold clues to the cause of the deadly crash, U.S. officials said on Thursday.

"Both are in excellent shape, the tapes are in good shape. There is useful data from both the black boxes," Dr Vernon Ellingstad, director of research and engineering at the National Transportation Safety Board told reporters.

The boxes, which despite being orange are often called black boxes, were displayed at NTSB headquarters. They appeared to have suffered no fire damage and were barely even dented despite the impact of the crash.
"We've seen lots of recorders in lots worse shape," Ellingstad said.
The Korean Air Lines plane slammed into a hillside early on Wednesday local time (Tuesday EDT/GMT) on approach to Guam's international airport with 254 people aboard.

The Boeing 747's cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and flight data recorder (FDR), which are housed in crush, burn and puncture resistant steel boxes installed in the tail section of the aircraft, were quickly recovered and arrived at the NTSB on Wednesday for analysis.
Engineers and technicians worked through the night on an initial inspection of the CVR which tapes the last 30 minutes of cockpit conversations and ambient noise.
The voices of the pilot and co-pilot can usually be heard along with the intercom and miscellaneous sounds such as engine noise, stall warnings and other clicks and pops.

A committee of NTSB officials and Federal Aviation Administration personnel, together with representatives of the plane's manufacturer and pilots' union, will listen to the recording and create a transcript.
Transcribing the information from the flight data recorder is more complex. The FDR on the Korean airliner recorded and stored 25 hours of flight information.
The result is a stream of digital signals that are meaningless until they are reconstructed using the NTSB's translation system. The board can then generate a computer-animated video of the flight.
Ellingstad told reporters the FDR on the Korean plane monitored 30 parameters -- or operating conditions -- such as time, altitude, airspeed and heading.
Some of the board's crash investigations have been hampered by FDRs on older aircraft which sometimes measure as few as 11 parameters.
Work on both KAL recorders continued on Thursday and the NTSB said no information on their contents was available.
Twenty-seven people survived the crash and 74 have been confirmed dead while 153 are still missing.
